common_name: Leucocarpa Nanking Cherry (White-Fruited Nanking Cherry Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Leucocarpa is a white-fruited color form of Nanking cherry, otherwise identical in culture to the species and benefiting from a second Nanking cherry planted nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun alongside a second Nanking cherry for reliable cross-pollination. Leucocarpa is a distinct white-fruited sport of Nanking cherry, bearing the same abundant early-summer crop as the common red form but with translucent, ivory-white to pale-yellow fruit that ripens a shade later and tends to escape the notice of fruit-eating birds that quickly strip red-fruited plants. The flavor is sweet with less of the tartness typical of the red form, making it pleasant for fresh eating as well as preserves. Like other Nanking cherry selections it flowers very early on a dense, spreading shrub and shrugs off poor, dry, or alkaline soils that would stress most stone fruits; prune lightly after harvest to keep the canopy open and productive.
sources: McKay Nursery -- Nanking Cherry Cultivars

common_name: Guthrie Chickasaw Plum (North Florida Large-Fruited Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root stock or container plants in early spring before bud break in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Guthrie is self-fruitful but crops more heavily with a second Chickasaw plum nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to light shade; Guthrie tolerates drought and neglect once its roots are established. Guthrie is a north Florida selection of Chickasaw plum chosen for unusually large, tangy-sweet, red-blushed yellow fruit approaching an inch and a half across, noticeably bigger than the typical wild Chickasaw plum crop, ripening in early to mid-summer and excellent fresh or cooked into jelly. The shrubby small tree forms a dense, thicketing, round-headed crown and, like the species, blooms very early in spring before leaf-out, providing one of the season's first nectar sources for native bees. It is fast growing, self-pollinating, and essentially carefree, asking only for good drainage and occasional removal of root suckers if a single-trunk form is wanted.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Mail Order Natives nursery notes

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Royalty is a named eastern mayhaw selection that benefits from a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a native wetland tree that thrives in the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most fruit trees struggle. Royalty is a named selection of eastern mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis), grown as a smaller, more spreading tree than many western mayhaw cultivars, producing clusters of bright red fruit in spring that ripen into the classic tart, aromatic berries prized for mayhaw jelly across the Gulf South. Like other mayhaws it can be affected by cedar-apple rust where eastern redcedar grows nearby, so siting away from cedars helps keep fruit and foliage clean. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar to ensure good cross-pollination, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years of planting.

common_name: Mason's Superberry Mayhaw (Texas Superberry, Early-Blooming Western Mayhaw)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Mason's Superberry is self-fruitful but sets a heavier crop with a second mayhaw cultivar nearby, since it is one of the earliest-flowering mayhaws and can otherwise bloom ahead of compatible pollinators.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a wetland native that tolerates the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most other fruit trees decline. Also sold as Texas Superberry, this East Texas selection of western mayhaw is one of the earliest-blooming named cultivars, opening flowers ahead of most other mayhaws in late winter, and produces large, deep red fruit with pink flesh that ripens by early May and hangs on the tree unusually long before dropping. The heavy, reliable crop and long hang time make harvest more forgiving than with cultivars that drop fruit quickly once ripe, though deer and other wildlife are drawn to it as readily as gardeners are. Expect bearing to begin within three to five years, with yields improving steadily as the tree matures.
sources: Bob Wells Nursery -- Mason's Superberry Mayhaw

common_name: Red Pearl Chilean Guava (INIA Chile Murtilla Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in a sheltered site with acidic, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Pearl was bred for larger, more uniform fruit than wild-collected Chilean guava.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltering from hard freezes in the cooler end of its range. Red Pearl is a patented selection released by Chile's national agricultural research institute (INIA) from a domestication program that began in the 1990s to bring wild-harvested murtilla into cultivated production, and it was chosen for dark red berries notably larger and more uniform than typical seedling Chilean guava. The compact, bushy, evergreen shrub bears its intensely aromatic, sweet-tart fruit over an extended late-season window, and the small, dark-green leaves make it as useful for clipped hedging as for fruit production. Harvest when berries are fully dark red and slightly soft for the best flavor, and expect several years of establishment before the plant reaches full bearing size.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP21273 -- Ugni molinae 'Red Pearl--INIA'

common_name: South Pearl Chilean Guava (INIA Chile Murtilla Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in a sheltered site with acidic, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; South Pearl is a sibling release to Red Pearl from the same Chilean murtilla breeding program.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltering from hard freezes in the cooler end of its range. South Pearl was released alongside Red Pearl under a plant patent from Chile's national agricultural research institute (INIA) as part of the same program to domesticate wild murtilla for commercial production, and shares the same compact, evergreen, hedge-friendly habit typical of cultivated Chilean guava selections. It bears the species' characteristically aromatic, sweet-tart berries, reminiscent of strawberry and guava, over a long ripening season into fall. As with other Chilean guava selections, several years of establishment are needed before the plant reaches full fruiting size, and a sheltered microclimate helps it perform at the cold edge of its hardiness range.

common_name: Jim Gerdemann Chilean Guava (Large Crimson-Fruited Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in a sheltered site with acidic, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; give consistent moisture, since this selection appreciates more water than typical Chilean guava.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping soil more consistently moist than most Chilean guava selections tolerate. Named for the horticulturist in whose garden it was discovered by nurseryman Ian Barclay, this selection is a lower, shrubbier, more rounded-leaved form of Chilean guava than the typical species, responding especially well to hedging and clipped forms. It produces large crimson fruit that ripens later in the season than many other selections, with the species' characteristic intense strawberry-watermelon aroma and flavor. Hardy to around 10F once established, it is best suited to sheltered gardens at the milder end of its zone range, where its evergreen foliage and drooping white summer flowers also make it a handsome ornamental hedge.

common_name: Daniecki Che (Male Pollinator for Mandarin Melon Berry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted-cutting tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Daniecki is a male selection grown solely to pollinate female che trees such as Darrow or Norris and does not itself bear edible fruit.

directions: Che is normally dioecious, and Daniecki is the named male selection most commonly planted to pollinate seedless female cultivars like Darrow and Norris, which otherwise set only a partial or unreliable crop without a compatible pollen source nearby. Its own flowers form small, pollen-bearing structures rather than edible fruit, so it is planted for function rather than harvest, typically one male for a small orchard block of female trees. Like other che selections it carries little winter chilling requirement and tolerates poor, dry, or alkaline soils far better than most fruiting trees, while young wood is thorny and benefits from early training to an open form. Plant within reasonable bee-flight distance of female che trees for best fruit set on the females.
sources: Cricket Hill Garden -- Che 'Daniecki' Male Pollinator

common_name: Edible Landscaping Seedless Che (Self-Fertile Mandarin Melon Berry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this self-fertile female selection sets a full seedless crop without a male pollinator nearby.

directions: Introduced and long propagated by Edible Landscaping nursery in Virginia, this selection is a self-fertile female che that reliably sets a full, seedless crop of maroon-red, mulberry-shaped fruit on its own, with no male tree required. The fig-and-watermelon-flavored fruit ripens over an extended late-summer-to-fall window and is best picked once fully soft, since underripe fruit is unpleasantly astringent. Grafted onto Osage orange rootstock, as is standard practice for che, the tree grows quickly into a large shrub or small standard tree that tolerates poor, dry, or alkaline soils far better than most fruiting trees and needs little winter chill to flower reliably. Young wood carries small thorns that diminish with age, so training to an open form early makes later harvest easier.
sources: Edible Landscaping -- Che Care Guide

common_name: Chuyskaya Sea Buckthorn (Star of Altai, Russian Low-Thorn Seaberry)

planting.note: Plant this Russian female cultivar in spring in full sun on lean, well-drained soil, with a male pollinator planted within about 50-100 feet.

directions: Chuyskaya, also marketed as Star of Altai, is a widely grown Russian sea buckthorn cultivar selected at breeding stations in the Altai region for noticeably fewer thorns than wild seaberry, which makes hand harvest considerably easier. It bears heavy clusters of bright orange, mildly tangy berries prized for juice, preserves, and vitamin-rich health products, and is counted among the sweeter and earlier-ripening seaberry selections available. Like all sea buckthorn it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its root system and thrives in poor, sandy, or coastal soils that would stunt most other fruiting shrubs, but it dislikes waterlogged ground. Being dioecious, it requires a male sea buckthorn nearby to set any fruit at all.
sources: Oak Summit Nursery -- Chuyskaya Sea Buckthorn

planting.note: Plant this female cultivar in spring in full sun on lean, well-drained soil, with a male pollinator planted within about 50-100 feet.

directions: Klavdija is a female sea buckthorn cultivar valued for producing heavy quantities of orange-red fruit on a shrub that is nearly thornless, letting berry-laden branches be picked by hand rather than stripped or cut, as is often necessary with thornier seaberry selections. Like other named sea buckthorn cultivars it forms a large, upright, nitrogen-fixing shrub that tolerates poor, sandy, or coastal soils and drought that would stunt most other fruiting plants, while resenting waterlogged sites. The tart, vitamin-C-rich berries are used for juice, syrup, and preserves. Being dioecious, Klavdija needs a male sea buckthorn planted nearby, since female plants set no fruit without pollination.

common_name: Regal Lingonberry (University of Wisconsin Dwarf Groundcover Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Regal is an extremely low, prostrate lingonberry that benefits from a nearby cultivar such as Red Pearl for best fruit set.

directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions. Regal was developed by the University of Wisconsin from open-pollinated seed of Finnish origin and selected for an unusually flat, prostrate habit, standing only two to four inches tall while spreading roughly two feet, making it one of the lowest-growing named lingonberry selections available for use as a true edible carpet groundcover. In warm-enough spring weather it can produce both a modest summer crop and a larger fall crop of medium-large berries, though yields are sparser than upright cultivars given the plant's diminutive size. Since lingonberries tolerate more shade than most fruiting plants, Regal works well tucked beneath blueberries, azaleas, or conifers where the soil is already suitably acidic; shear lightly every few years to keep the mat dense and vigorous.
sources: Raintree Nursery -- Regal Lingonberry

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Scarlet is a compact, low-growing lingonberry valued as a reliable pollinizer for other named cultivars.

directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions. Scarlet is a dwarf, evergreen lingonberry selection standing just four to eight inches tall, producing a reasonable quantity of medium-sized, cranberry-flavored red berries on its branch tips while also serving as a dependable pollinizer that boosts fruit set on neighboring lingonberry cultivars. Its diminutive, spreading habit makes it as useful for ornamental edging and container growing as for harvest, and like other lingonberries it tolerates more shade than most fruiting plants provided the soil stays consistently acidic. Shear lightly every few years to rejuvenate growth and keep the planting dense.
sources: Raintree Nursery -- Scarlet Lingonberry
